Here's an attempt at a short version: It's a power struggle between press and consumers, fighting for the average joe to have a voice in the industry. >Here< is a cool comment from reddit that touches upon similar concepts. Given that GamerGate has been given this silly woman-hating identity, it makes sense to try to dispel it, to make people question it, and relieve the voices of GamerGate from any identity, and keep it focused on the ideas.

The long:

GamerGate is a hashtag, a megaphone that literally anyone can pick up and use. And, in fact, we have seen places hire several dozen (maybe more) bots to spew anti-women/radical right-wing/whatever bullshit through the megaphone, in order to try and taint the "group". Of course, it's not really an organised group. "GamerGaters" is just a list of people who happen to have picked up the megaphone and spoken through it. The reason they are able to get things done with it is because of the way twitter enhances trends.

Let's say there's a trend. People are trying to draw attention to an issue (say, TFYC), so they are talking about it on social media like twitter. twitter will pick that up and broadcast it, which propagates the message, the voice. More people will come and pick up the megaphone and say the same things. They will do this not because they "belong" to it, it's that it just so happens to involve an idea they share/believe in. For example: they want to help women in gaming — whether it be simply to refute the press' accusations about "GamerGate" being misogynistic (i.e. to prove a point), or actually to help women, or both.

Why would they care about what the press has to say about the "group" if it's not a group, and they aren't truly responsible for the bad stuff the press says about them? Well, because when the press smear the megaphone, they take away its power — they want to make it faulty/malfunctional so that nobody who speaks through it gets listened to. The press want to take away these people's voices because they do not like/agree with what they are saying... or, they want all of the voice, the power.

I don't really know how you can directly fight that, to be honest, but those people who write the sarcastic headlines you are talking about seem to think that dispelling the claims levied against the megaphone is a good way to do it. And I agree, I think it does go some way towards re-empowering the tag.

GamerGate isn't anti-feminist or anti-diversity-in-games. There are some trolls and such puppets who use the tag on twitter to sign their attempts at harassing people, but if you go visit some if the GG sub verses, you'll see discussion on politics, journalism ethics, and the follies of those have aligned themselves as enemies to "gamers".

Many modern internet feminists have labeled GG as misogynistic, in order to silence debate about ethics in games journalism, which is what GG is actually about. In fact, Christina Hoff-Summers, a prominent feminist academic, was warmly welcomed by GamerGaters in DC at a meetup to discuss the issues. That meeting was interrupted by a bomb threat from a concerned anti-GGer, and police had to evacuate a building.
